Finally, we present the relationship between perceived originality and functional quality and the differences between raters, and we summarize the main findings.

Divergent Thinking and the Aesthetic Evaluation of Chairs

Mean DT was 2.46 (SD = 0.35) on Ocsai's 1-5 originality scale. All chairs were perceived as moderately to highly original. Mean originality ratings ranged from 4.67 for Chair 1 to 5.59 for Chair 4. Participants rated functional quality near the midpoint of the scale (M = 3.59-4.29; Table 1). Table 1 shows that chairs differed more in perceived originality than in functional quality. As preregistered, we correlated DT with each chair's overall rating (Table 2). Only Chair 1 showed a nominally significant correlation (r = .24, p = .017). That correlation did not survive Holm correction (p = .085). For Chairs 2-5, the correlations ranged from r = -.08 to .12 (all p ≥ .24). For Chair 4 (the chair rated as most original), the correlation was r = .11, p = .30.

DT accounted for at most 6% of the variance in any chair's rating. With covariates, the Chair 1 effect was B = 0.15 per SD, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.30], p = .065. These estimates did not depend on the covariate specification. No chair reached significance after Holm correction, with or without covariates (Table S5). Table 2 shows that the preregistered hypothesis was not supported. A linear mixed model on all 485 ratings confirmed this. DT did not predict the overall rating (B = 0.05 per SD, p = .53), the originality rating (B = 0.08, p = .54), or functional quality (B = 0.04, p = .62). The effect of DT did not differ across chairs for the overall rating (χ²(4) = 6.60, p = .16) or the originality rating (χ²(4) = 1.46, p = .83). The same held for functional quality (χ²(4) = 6.16, p = .19). All chair-specific estimates had 95% CIs that included zero.

Creative Personality, Openness, and Demographic Factors

GCPS scores (M = 6.07, SD = 3.71, range -4 to 13) were not significantly associated with DT (r = .01, p = .96; Table S4). They were also unrelated to the ratings of the individual chairs reported in Table 1 (r = -.11 to .07, all p ≥ .29). The DT × creative personality interaction was statistically significant, B = -0.18 per SD × SD, 95% CI [-0.34, -0.01], p = .039. Its direction, however, was opposite to the hypothesized amplifying effect. DT was positively related to ratings at low creative personality (-1 SD: B = 0.29, p = .020) and unrelated at high creative personality (+1 SD: B = -0.06, p = .60).

Gender did not predict ratings of any chair (all p ≥ .21). Study year was unrelated to ratings of all chairs (all p ≥ .26). Hobbies were unrelated to all ratings (all p ≥ .34).

Openness to experience was associated with more favorable ratings across chairs, B = 0.24 per SD, p = .003. It explained 8.4% of the variance in participants' mean ratings. This association did not differ across chairs, χ²(4) = 4.22, p = .38. The association remained significant when DT and all covariates were included, B = 0.21 per SD, p = .016 (Table S5).

Openness was not significantly related to DT, r = .19, p = .057 (Table S4).

Coupling of Perceived Originality and Functional Quality

Perceived originality and functional quality were positively correlated for Chair 3, r = .29, 95% CI [.07, .50], with a Holm-corrected p = .020. The correlation was nominally significant for Chair 5, r = .23 [-.02, .45], p = .025, but not after correction (p = .10). It was positive but not significant for Chair 4, r = .19 [.00, .36], p = .065. It was absent for Chair 1 (r = .07 [-.15, .30]) and Chair 2 (r = -.07 [-.31, .16]). The strength of coupling differed across the five chairs, χ²(4) = 11.69, p = .020. Note. (A) Estimated effects of a 1-SD increase in DT on the originality rating (orange) and the functional-quality rating (blue) for each chair. Estimates are from a linear mixed model with a random intercept per participant. Covariates were cultural orientation, gender, hobbies, and study year. (B) Pearson correlation between the originality and functional-quality ratings for each chair, with 95% bootstrap CIs (5,000 resamples). Red indicates significance after Holm correction. Error bars indicate 95% CIs; n = 97.

Figure 2 contrasts two sets of associations. Figure 2A shows the associations between DT and chair ratings. Figure 2B shows the relationships between perceived originality and functional quality across the five chairs. The estimated associations involving DT were small and not statistically significant (Figure 2A). By contrast, the association between perceived originality and functional quality differed across the five chairs (Figure 2B; χ²(4) = 11.69, p = .020). The strongest positive correlations were observed for the Panton Chair (r = .29) and Harp Chair (r = .23), although only the Panton Chair correlation remained significant after Holm correction. No statistically significant correlation was detected for the Calvet Armchair or Tube Chair. These findings indicate stimulus-specific variation in participants' evaluations but do not identify the design characteristics underlying that variation.

Figure 3 shows how the CPSS items cluster for each chair. Note. Average-linkage hierarchical clustering of the CPSS items using 1 -r. Originality and trendsetting are shown in purple. n = 97.

Figure 3 shows that the two novelty items never formed a separate cluster. In Chairs 2, 4, and 5, originality was the last item to join the cluster tree. Perceived originality emerged as a distinct evaluative component from the functional items. In Chair 3, by contrast, originality joined the functional items before the ordered item did, consistent with its coupling with functional quality. Trendsetting and influential, the germinal items, clustered early with the functional items in every chair. Participants appear to have read these items as signs of a product's impact rather than of its novelty. This pattern supports using the originality rating as an index of perceived novelty (O'Quin & Besemer, 2006). As illustrated in Figure 4A, evaluator characteristics, including DT, creative personality, cultural orientation, gender, and study year, accounted for little variance in aesthetic evaluation. Openness to experience was associated with higher ratings of all designs.

Stable differences between raters accounted for more variance than any measured evaluator characteristic. In contrast, the coupling of perceived originality and functional quality varied across designs (Figure 4B). Coupling was highest for chairs with intermediate perceived originality and lower at both extremes. This pattern descriptively resembles the inverted-U relation proposed by the MAYA principle (Hekkert et al., 2003). The Tube Chair deviated most from this pattern, whereas the Consumer's Rest chair showed moderate coupling despite high perceived originality. Overall, chair evaluations varied more with the design being evaluated than with evaluators' DT. Design features were not manipulated, and creative ability was indexed only by DT. These findings therefore do not establish that design causally shapes evaluation.

Discussion

Creativity is frequently conceptualized as involving both generative and evaluative processes (Khalil & Moustafa, 2022; Silvia, 2008). Yet the association between DT and evaluative skill is small (Guo et al., 2022). Research on aesthetic appreciation further highlights perceptual, cognitive, and contextual influences on responses to designed objects (Leder et al., 2004; Leder & Nadal, 2014). Against this background, the present study examined whether DT and other evaluator characteristics were associated with aesthetic evaluation. We operationalized aesthetic evaluation through CPSS-based judgments of creativity-related attributes for five chair designs (Figure 1). A second aim was to explore whether the association between perceived originality and functional quality varied across chairs. We discuss the findings in relation to creative cognition, the MAYA principle, and product semantics. We did not measure aesthetic preference, product typicality, or objective design characteristics independently.

We first assessed whether DT was associated with participants' overall CPSS ratings of the chairs. The preregistered hypothesis was not supported. After correction for multiple comparisons, none of the chair-specific associations remained significant (Table 2; Figure 2A).

Creative personality was not associated with overall chair ratings. Contrary to our hypothesis, it also did not strengthen the relationship between DT and these ratings. The interaction between DT and creative personality ran in the opposite direction to what was predicted. DT was related to ratings only among participants with low creative personality scores. As this reversed moderation was not anticipated, it requires replication. The absence of a reliable DT effect aligns with the small meta-analytic association between DT and evaluative skill (Guo et al., 2022). Participants' judgments of the insightfulness of their own responses were also unrelated to the originality of those responses (Table S3). This result is consistent with evidence that individuals identify their own best ideas only moderately well (Silvia, 2008). A nonsignificant association does not demonstrate that idea generation and evaluation rely on distinct processes.

However, the present data provide no evidence that originality in idea generation translates into differences in product evaluation.

Chair 1, the Calvet Armchair by Antoni Gaudí (1902), was the only design whose rating correlated with DT prior to correction. This association was attributable to the operability item rather than the originality item (Table S6). Participants with higher DT rated this chair as more usable, but not as more original. The chair combines a conventional configuration with irregular, carved organic forms. Its usability is plausible but not immediately apparent. The AUT requires individuals to identify uses beyond an object's conventional function, thereby counteracting functional fixedness (Chrysikou & Weisberg, 2005; Duncker, 1945). Individuals with higher DT may more readily perceive the affordances of an unusual form (Gibson, 1979; Norman, 2013).

The Calvet Armchair was also the only historical design in the set. Its novelty may have been perceived as craftsmanship rather than functional innovation, which could explain why its originality and functional quality were not associated. This interpretation aligns with evidence that individuals value historical solutions alongside innovative ones (Reis et al., 2025). The association was neither predicted nor robust to correction. It should therefore be treated as a hypothesis for future confirmatory testing.

Next, we explored whether the association between perceived originality and functional quality varied across the five chairs. The results indicated significant variation in this association across chairs (Figure 2B). Coupling was strongest for the Panton and Harp chairs, which had intermediate perceived originality. The association was weaker for the Consumer's

Rest chair and absent for the Calvet Armchair and Tube Chair. This pattern resembles the inverted-U relationship between novelty and preference reported for chairs (Hung & Chen, 2012) and the curvilinear effect of typicality reported for other products (Blijlevens et al., 2012).

One interpretation is that, within an acceptable range, novelty signals good design, whereas beyond this range novelty is recognized as originality but evaluated separately from function. The Tube Chair, whose modular cylinders lack the conventional structure of a chair, supports this interpretation. However, the present study did not measure typicality or acceptability or establish an empirical acceptability threshold. This interpretation remains a hypothesis for studies that measure these constructs directly (Blijlevens et al., 2012; Hekkert et al., 2003). The item structure supports this account: originality formed a component distinct from the functional items in most chairs but joined them for the Panton Chair (Figure 3). With only five designs, these patterns remain descriptive.

Figure 4 integrates these findings. Evaluators differed in their overall level of appreciation, and stable rater differences represented the largest systematic source of variance (Figure 4A). In contrast, the coupling of perceived originality and functional quality varied across designs (Figure 4B). Openness to experience accounted for part of the variance in rating levels, as participants with higher openness rated all chairs more favorably. Openness is the personality domain most closely associated with aesthetic sensitivity (McCrae, 2007). Cultural orientation showed a similar but nonsignificant tendency toward higher overall ratings, without a chair-specific pattern. Consumer-based assessment should explicitly model rater effects, so that differences in response level are not mistaken for differences in taste (Horn & Salvendy, 2006).

Practical Implications

These findings do not support the assumption that consumers with higher DT respond more favorably to creative designs. Product appearance influences consumer response through perceived function and visual appeal (Bloch, 1995; Crilly et al., 2004).

Three implications follow for product evaluation, prototype testing, and consumer research. They correspond to the user-centered testing stage of design thinking (Brown, 2008; Liedtka, 2015).

First, the lack of a reliable association between DT and product evaluations suggests that DT performance alone should not be a criterion for selecting product evaluators. Design teams may benefit more from evaluators with diverse perspectives than from evaluators selected for high DT performance.

Second, the design-specific relationship between perceived originality and functional quality highlights the value of assessing these attributes separately during product evaluation.

Rather than relying exclusively on overall creativity ratings, designers can examine how originality and functionality are perceived across alternative concepts. Such assessments may help identify differences in how users interpret product attributes and inform further investigation during prototype development. Averaging CPSS dimensions into a single creativity score may obscure these differences (Horn & Salvendy, 2006; O'Quin & Besemer, 2006).

Third, the association between openness to experience and overall product ratings highlights the importance of considering evaluator characteristics when interpreting consumer feedback. In comparative product testing, accounting for individual rating tendencies may help distinguish general differences in evaluation levels from differences in responses to particular designs. Consumer-rating studies may treat both raters and stimuli as random factors (Judd et al., 2012). Together, these implications encourage more differentiated approaches to product assessment that consider both perceived design attributes and evaluator characteristics.

Limitations and Future Directions

The findings should be considered within the context of the study's sample and research design. Evaluating five selected chair designs provides insights into how perceived originality and functional quality relate across different product stimuli. However, a survey error removed one chair, and the remaining five designs were presented as photographs. Functional quality was therefore inferred from appearance rather than from use. Future research could extend this approach to a broader range of products and examine how specific design characteristics, such as novelty, typicality, and visual complexity, contribute to aesthetic evaluations.

The study examined aesthetic evaluation through CPSS-based judgments of creativityrelated product attributes. Future studies could complement these measures with validated assessments of aesthetic pleasure (Blijlevens et al., 2017), preference, and perceived usability to provide a more comprehensive understanding of product evaluation. Such research could investigate the relationships proposed by the MAYA principle by directly measuring novelty, typicality, and acceptability (Hekkert et al., 2003).

Finally, the study involved 97 university students and assessed DT only through the originality of AUT responses. Future research could extend the investigation to different age groups, cultural contexts, and levels of design expertise, while incorporating broader measures of creative cognition. The internal consistency of the openness (α = .57) and creative personality (KR-20 = .61) scores was relatively low, which may have attenuated their associations with ratings (Nunnally & Bernstein, 1994). The stimulus-specific findings were exploratory. Larger, preregistered studies could further examine the relationships between evaluator characteristics, perceived product attributes, and aesthetic evaluation.

The sample included students of many nationalities at an international university, broadening the cultural range of the evaluators. Extending this design to older adults, nonstudent and professional evaluators, and other cultural contexts would test how far the findings generalize across people (Miller et al., 2025). Sampling chairs beyond one collection would test their generalization across designs (Judd et al., 2012). The following directions build on these opportunities.

We assessed cultural orientation with a binary self-classification, providing a starting point for studying a multidimensional construct (Markus & Kitayama, 1991; Triandis & Gelfand, 1998; Vignoles et al., 2016). The cultural diversity of the present sample suggests that continuous measures of self-construal would be a promising refinement (Miller et al., 2025; Singelis, 1994). Employing validated, full-length measures of openness would clarify its role in appreciating novel products (Costa & McCrae, 1992).

Extending these ratings to consumer decisions is a logical next step. Measures such as purchase intention or willingness to pay would help establish the practical relevance of these effects (Bloch, 1995). Field studies with real products would test whether coupling originality and function predicts market acceptance (Horn & Salvendy, 2006).

Conclusions

DT, indexed by the originality of AUT responses, was not associated with how individuals evaluated five chair designs, and creative personality did not strengthen this relationship. Openness to experience was associated with more favorable ratings of all chairs but did not alter which designs were preferred. The association between perceived originality and perceived function varied across designs. This pattern is consistent with, but does not directly test, the MAYA principle and design-thinking accounts (Dorst, 2011; Hekkert et al., 2003). Within the limits of this sample and stimulus set, generating original ideas and evaluating creative products appear to be dissociable. Creativity research and product evaluation may benefit from assessing novelty and function separately and from explicitly modeling differences among raters.

Differences Between Raters

Participants differed substantially in their overall rating levels. Stable rater differences are consistent tendencies of individual participants to rate all chairs higher or lower than others.

They correspond to the variance of the participant random intercepts and accounted for 38% of the variance in overall ratings (random-intercept variance = 0.44; residual variance = 0.72).

Individualistically oriented participants tended to rate all chairs higher, but this difference was not significant (B = 0.31, p = .070). After ratings were centered within each participant, cultural orientation had no effect, Wald χ²(5) = 3.09, p = .69. Nor did it interact with chair, χ²(4) = 2.47, p = .65. The preregistered and exploratory results were unchanged in the full sample of 108 respondents (Table S1). In that sample, higher ratings among individualistically oriented participants were significant (p = .032).
